def: Machines collectively, or the components of a machine.
ex: Workers must wear protective yellow helmets when operating heavy industrial machinery in the warehouse.
nat: The agricultural cooperative purchased modern machinery to speed up autumn grain harvesting.

mis.bad: The company bought new machineries yesterday.
mis.good: The company bought new machinery yesterday.
mis.why: "Machinery" is uncountable; never add an "-s" or use "machineries".

def: The state of being mentally ill, or extremely foolish behavior.
ex: Driving through a severe blizzard without snow tires is complete madness on mountain passes.
nat: During holiday sales, the downtown shopping mall turns into utter madness and chaos.

mis.bad: It is a madness to drive so fast.
mis.good: It is madness to drive so fast.
mis.why: Omit the indefinite article: say "it is madness", not "a madness".

def: Relating to, using, or resembling magic; wonderful or enchanting.
ex: Watching the aurora borealis illuminate the night sky was truly a magical travel experience.
nat: The children listened with open mouths to the magical fairy tale about enchanted castles.

mis.bad: We spent a magic evening together.
mis.good: We spent a magical evening together.
mis.why: Use "magical" for figurative or delightful experiences; "magic" usually refers to literal illusionist acts.

def: A civil officer or lay judge who administers the law, especially in minor offenses.
ex: The local magistrate ordered the landlord to refund the tenant's security deposit immediately.
nat: Minor traffic infractions are usually handled quickly before a city magistrate rather than a jury.

mis.bad: The case was presented to a magistrated judge.
mis.good: The case was presented to a local magistrate.
mis.why: "Magistrate" is a noun referring to the official; do not invent "magistrated".

def: To make something appear larger than it is, especially with a lens, or intensify.
ex: The laboratory microscope will magnify tiny bacteria cells up to one thousand times clearly.
nat: Spreading unverified rumors online will only magnify unnecessary panic during public health emergencies.

mis.bad: The lens magnifies up the picture.
mis.good: The lens magnifies the picture.
mis.why: Do not add "up" after "magnify"; it takes a direct object.

def: The great size or extent of something, or a numerical measure of earthquake intensity.
ex: Government officials did not immediately realize the tremendous magnitude of the environmental disaster.
nat: A powerful earthquake of magnitude seven struck off the southern coast early this morning.

mis.bad: An earthquake with magnitude seven occurred.
mis.good: An earthquake of magnitude seven occurred.
mis.why: Use "of magnitude [number]", not "with magnitude".

def: Being the first of its kind; inaugural.
ex: The luxury ocean liner departed Southampton on its historic maiden voyage across the Atlantic.
nat: The newly elected senator delivered her maiden speech before a crowded congressional chamber yesterday.

mis.bad: The ship made its initial maiden voyage.
mis.good: The ship made its maiden voyage.
mis.why: "Maiden voyage" already means the first trip; avoid combining with "initial".

def: Belonging to or characteristic of the prevailing current or direction of activity or style.
ex: Electric vehicles have moved rapidly from a niche hobby into mainstream consumer adoption worldwide.
nat: Alternative indie musicians often prefer independent record labels over large mainstream media conglomerates.

mis.bad: The idea entered into the mainstream.
mis.good: The idea entered the mainstream.
mis.why: "Enter" takes a direct object: "entered the mainstream", not "into".

def: Having or showing impressive beauty or dignity.
ex: Tourists marveled at the majestic snow-capped peaks rising above the emerald green alpine lake.
nat: An eagle soared gracefully over the deep river canyon in truly majestic flight yesterday.

mis.bad: The palace has a majestic appearance of outside.
mis.good: The palace has a majestic appearance on the outside.
mis.why: Say "on the outside", not "of outside".

def: The intention or desire to do evil; ill will.
ex: The journalist stated clearly that her critical investigation was conducted without any personal malice.
nat: The cybercriminal demonstrated clear malice by deploying ransomware that crippled local hospital systems.

mis.bad: He did it for malice.
mis.good: He did it out of malice / with malice.
mis.why: The standard idiom is "do something out of malice".

def: Characterized by malice; intending or intended to do harm.
ex: The security team blocked suspicious incoming traffic originating from a known malicious server network.
nat: Spreading malicious rumors about colleagues can lead to disciplinary termination in corporate settings.

mis.bad: He sent me a malicious link in intention to hack.
mis.good: He sent me a malicious link with the intention of hacking.
mis.why: Say "with the intention of + -ing".

def: To speak about someone in a spitefully critical manner.
ex: Competitors tried unfairly to malign the startup's reputation by posting anonymous fabricated negative reviews.
nat: Public figures often find it difficult to stop tabloids that deliberately malign their families.

mis.bad: He maligned about his former manager.
mis.good: He maligned his former manager.
mis.why: "Malign" is transitive; do not insert the preposition "about".

def: Able to be hammered or pressed permanently out of shape without breaking, or easily influenced.
ex: Pure gold is an extraordinarily malleable metal that can be hammered into microscopic sheets.
nat: Young children possess remarkably malleable minds that absorb new foreign languages with incredible ease.

mis.bad: The iron becomes malleable with high temperatures.
mis.good: The iron becomes malleable at high temperatures.
mis.why: Use "at high temperatures", not "with".

def: Huge; gigantic.
ex: Organizing the international climate conference proved to be a mammoth undertaking for the committee.
nat: The tech conglomerate invested a mammoth twenty billion dollars into generative neural infrastructure projects.

mis.bad: It was a mammoth of a project.
mis.good: It was a mammoth project / a mammoth task.
mis.why: Use "mammoth" directly as an adjective before the noun: "a mammoth task".

def: Able to be controlled, handled, or dealt with without undue difficulty.
ex: Breaking large software feature requests into small manageable user stories prevents developer burnout effectively.
nat: With regular daily study habits, achieving conversational English fluency becomes a completely manageable goal.

mis.bad: The workload is manageable for do.
mis.good: The workload is manageable to handle / manageable.
mis.why: Avoid "manageable for do"; use "manageable" alone or "manageable to handle".

def: The process of dealing with or controlling things or people, or the executive team.
ex: Effective time management is the most valuable professional skill for remote software engineering teams.
nat: Senior management decided to approve flexible hybrid working hours starting the first of January.

mis.bad: I want to speak with the gerency.
mis.good: I want to speak with management / the manager.
mis.why: In Portuguese "gerência" translates to "management" or "the manager", never "gerency".

def: Required by law or rules; compulsory.
ex: Wearing safety goggles and closed-toe footwear is strictly mandatory inside the chemistry research laboratory.
nat: Attending the Monday morning engineering sprint planning meeting is mandatory for all team developers.

mis.bad: This meeting is mandatory for everyone attend.
mis.good: This meeting is mandatory for everyone to attend.
mis.why: Remember the infinitive "to": "mandatory for everyone to attend".

def: To clear or show a quality or feeling by one's acts or appearance; demonstrate.
ex: Chronic workplace anxiety can easily manifest as physical symptoms like persistent insomnia and headaches.
nat: The team's dedication manifested in their spotless record of delivering every project on time.

mis.bad: The stress manifested on physical pain.
mis.good: The stress manifested as physical pain.
mis.why: Use "manifest as [symptoms]", not "on".

def: To handle or control a tool or mechanism, or influence people unscrupulously.
ex: The skilled surgeon used robotic arms to manipulate tiny surgical instruments inside the patient.
nat: Untrustworthy leaders often try to manipulate public opinion through emotional speeches and false claims.

mis.bad: He manipulated with the database.
mis.good: He manipulated the database.
mis.why: "Manipulate" is transitive; do not use "with".

def: The human race; human beings considered collectively.
ex: Landing astronauts safely on the moon was described as a giant leap for all mankind.
nat: Curing infectious viral diseases remains one of the greatest collaborative challenges facing modern mankind.

mis.bad: The mankind must protect the planet.
mis.good: Mankind must protect the planet.
mis.why: Never use the definite article "the" before "mankind" when referring to humanity.

def: Having a human crew; operated by people.
ex: Space agencies are actively preparing their first manned mission to the Martian planetary surface.
nat: The security checkpoint is manned twenty-four hours a day by trained private security personnel.

mis.bad: The station is manned by five persons.
mis.good: The station is manned by five people.
mis.why: Use "five people" rather than "five persons" in natural English.

def: A way in which a thing is done or happens, or a person's outward behavior.
ex: She answered all the difficult interview questions in a calm, confident, and professional manner.
nat: Teaching young children table manners early helps them behave politely during formal family dinners.

mis.bad: He did it in this manner of way.
mis.good: He did it in this manner / in this way.
mis.why: Do not say "manner of way"; use either "manner" or "way".

def: A large, impressive, and stately house.
ex: The wealthy technology investor purchased a historic stone mansion overlooking the Pacific Ocean coastline.
nat: Tourists took guided bus tours through Beverly Hills to view celebrity mansions and gardens.

mis.bad: He lives in a big mansion house.
mis.good: He lives in a big mansion.
mis.why: "Mansion" already implies a house; omit the redundant word "house".

pt: manual de instruções / guia do usuário
def: A book of instructions, especially for operating a machine or learning a subject.
ex: Always consult the official user manual before attempting to disassemble any internal computer components.
nat: The airline provides pilots with an exhaustive flight operations manual for every aircraft model.

mis.bad: I read the manual of instructions.
mis.good: I read the instruction manual.
mis.why: Use the compound noun "instruction manual" rather than "manual of instructions".

def: A book, document, or piece of music written by hand rather than typed or printed.
ex: The author submitted her completed fantasy novel manuscript to three major literary publishers yesterday.
nat: Historians carefully preserved ancient parchment manuscripts discovered inside dry desert monastery caves.

mis.bad: She gave the manuscript to the editor by hand.
mis.good: She submitted her manuscript to the editor.
mis.why: Collocate naturally with "submit a manuscript to an editor".

def: A long-distance running race of strictly 26.2 miles, or an arduous long task.
ex: She trained rigorously for six months before completing her first Boston Marathon under four hours.
nat: The engineering team completed a grueling twenty-hour hackathon marathon to ship the product feature.

mis.bad: He ran in the marathon of Chicago.
mis.good: He ran the Chicago Marathon.
mis.why: Say "ran the Chicago Marathon" without awkward prepositions.

def: A hard crystalline metamorphic form of limestone, or a small glass ball used in games.
ex: The museum lobby features gleaming white Italian marble floors and tall polished classical pillars.
nat: Children used to spend hours playing marble games on dusty school playgrounds during recess.

mis.bad: The statue was sculpted in marble stone.
mis.good: The statue was sculpted in marble.
mis.why: "Marble" is already a stone; omit "stone".

pt: marchar / desfilar / avançar a passos largos
def: To walk with regular, measured steps, often in a group or as a military unit.
ex: Thousands of peaceful citizens decided to march through downtown streets demanding cleaner renewable energy.
nat: Soldiers marched in perfect unison across the paved courtyard during the annual national parade.

mis.bad: They marched through the streets by protesting.
mis.good: They marched through the streets in protest.
mis.why: Use the fixed prepositional phrase "in protest", not "by protesting".

def: Of secondary or minor importance; not central, or relating to a border.
ex: The new software update resulted in only a marginal improvement in overall battery efficiency.
nat: Economists analyze marginal cost to determine the optimal production level for profitable manufacturing operations.

mis.bad: The change had a marginal effect to performance.
mis.good: The change had a marginal effect on performance.
mis.why: Use "effect on [something]", not "effect to".

pt: margem de lucro / marcação de código
def: The amount added to the cost price of goods to cover overhead and profit.
ex: The boutique clothing retailer applies a standard hundred percent markup on wholesale designer imported shoes.
nat: HyperText Markup Language forms the foundational building block for constructing modern accessible website pages.

mis.bad: The store puts a high mark up in prices.
mis.good: The store adds a high markup to prices.
mis.why: Write as a single noun "markup" and use "add a markup to prices".

def: Appropriate to war; warlike; relating to fighting or armed forces.
ex: Practicing traditional Japanese martial arts helps students develop physical discipline, mental focus, and respect.
nat: The prime minister declared martial law across the capital after violent civil unrest erupted.

mis.bad: He practices martial arts since five years.
mis.good: He has been practicing martial arts for five years.
mis.why: Use the present perfect with "for [duration]", not "since [duration]".

def: To be filled with wonder or astonishment.
ex: Astronomers still marvel at the breathtaking complexity and immense scale of the observable universe.
nat: Tourists marvel at the ancient stone pyramids standing silently against the golden Egyptian desert.

mis.bad: We marveled with the view from the top.
mis.good: We marveled at the view from the top.
mis.why: Always use "marvel at [something]", not "with".

def: Causing great wonder; extraordinary; extremely good.
ex: We had a marvelous weekend exploring the cobblestone alleys and artisan cafes of Lisbon.
nat: The pianist gave a marvelous performance that earned a standing ovation from the entire theater.

mis.bad: It was a marvelous for us.
mis.good: It was marvelous for us / We had a marvelous time.
mis.why: "Marvelous" is an adjective, so do not say "a marvelous" without a noun.

def: Having qualities or an appearance traditionally associated with men.
ex: The interior designer opted for dark leather furniture and brushed metal accents for a masculine feel.
nat: In Portuguese grammar, all nouns are categorized as possessing either masculine or feminine grammatical gender.

mis.bad: The word table has a masculine gender.
mis.good: In Portuguese, the word for table has feminine gender.
mis.why: Be careful not to mix grammatical gender with gender identity.

def: A covering for all or part of the face, worn as a disguise or for protection.
ex: Carpenters wear a protective dust mask when sanding hardwood floors inside an enclosed residential room.
nat: Venetian carnival participants wore ornate handcrafted masks adorned with golden feathers and delicate jewels.

mis.bad: Put the mask in your face.
mis.good: Put the mask on your face / wear a mask.
mis.why: Use "put on a mask" or "wear a mask on your face", not "in your face".

def: A coherent, typically large body of matter with no definite shape, or a large number.
ex: A dense mass of storm clouds formed rapidly over the mountains during the late afternoon.
nat: The innovative electric car entered mass production after factory robotics finished installation and testing.

mis.bad: The company entered in mass production.
mis.good: The company entered mass production.
mis.why: "Enter" takes a direct object without "in": "entered mass production".

def: An indiscriminate and brutal slaughter of many people, or a crushing sporting defeat.
ex: Historians documented the horrific civilian massacre that occurred during the final weeks of the war.
nat: The local soccer derby turned into an embarrassing five-nil massacre for the visiting team.

mis.bad: The battle was a massacre of soldiers.
mis.good: The battle was a massacre.
mis.why: Avoid clumsy redundant phrases like "massacre of soldiers" when context is clear.

def: Large and heavy or solid; exceptionally large, severe, or extensive.
ex: The sudden power outage caused massive disruption to subway transit systems throughout the entire metropolitan area.
nat: The startup received a massive surge in website traffic after being featured on national television.

mis.bad: There was a massive of people.
mis.good: There was a massive crowd / a massive number of people.
mis.why: "Massive" is an adjective and cannot be used with "a massive of".

def: Comprehensive knowledge or skill in a subject or accomplishment.
ex: Achieving true mastery of conversational English requires hundreds of hours of deliberate speaking practice.
nat: Her technical mastery of the piano allowed her to play complex concertos without sheet music.

mis.bad: He has mastery on English.
mis.good: He has mastery of English / has mastered English.
mis.why: Say "mastery of [a language/subject]", not "mastery on".

def: A contest in which people or teams compete, or a stick for lighting fires.
ex: Thousands of enthusiastic fans attended the exciting championship football match at the national stadium.
nat: He struck a wooden match against the sandpaper strip to light the scented candle.

mis.bad: We watched the football game match.
mis.good: We watched the football match / the football game.
mis.why: Use either "match" or "game", never combine them as "game match".

def: Relating to a mother, especially during pregnancy or shortly after childbirth.
ex: Good access to prenatal healthcare significantly reduces maternal mortality rates in rural developing regions.
nat: She felt a strong maternal instinct to protect her newborn twin daughters from any harm.

mis.bad: My maternal grandfather was born on Italy.
mis.good: My maternal grandfather was born in Italy.
mis.why: Use "in Italy" for countries, not "on Italy".

def: The period during pregnancy and shortly after childbirth, or motherhood.
ex: The company offers six months of paid maternity leave to all full-time female employees.
nat: She gave birth to healthy twin boys at the downtown private maternity hospital yesterday.

mis.bad: She is on licency maternity.
mis.good: She is on maternity leave.
mis.why: Translate Portuguese "licença-maternidade" as "maternity leave".

def: Of, relating to, or using the science of numbers, quantities, and shapes.
ex: Cryptography relies heavily on rigorous mathematical proofs to guarantee data privacy and system security.
nat: The algorithm uses a complex mathematical model to predict severe changes in weather patterns.

mis.bad: He solved the problem with a mathematic formula.
mis.good: He solved the problem with a mathematical formula.
mis.why: Use the adjective "mathematical" before nouns, not "mathematic".

def: An environment or material in which something develops, or a rectangular array of numbers.
ex: Product managers use a prioritization matrix to decide which engineering tasks deliver the highest impact.
nat: Graphics processing units multiply large numerical matrices at blinding speeds to render realistic video game graphics.

mis.bad: They organized the tasks in a matrix of priorities.
mis.good: They organized the tasks in a prioritization matrix.
mis.why: Use the compound noun "prioritization matrix" for natural business English.

def: To make as large or great as possible, or make the best use of.
ex: Remote software workers often use time-blocking productivity methods to maximize their daily deep-focus hours.
nat: You should click the top-right window button to maximize the spreadsheet across the entire monitor.

mis.bad: We need to maximize up our results.
mis.good: We need to maximize our results.
mis.why: Do not say "maximize up"; "maximize" already means increasing to the highest level.

def: As great, high, or intense as possible or permitted.
ex: The maximum speed limit on rural interstate highways is typically seventy-five miles per hour.
nat: The auditorium has a maximum legal seating capacity of four hundred people during concerts.

mis.bad: The max capacity was exceeded.
mis.good: The maximum capacity was exceeded.
mis.why: In formal or written contexts, use the full word "maximum" rather than the abbreviation "max".

def: A network of paths and hedges designed as a puzzle through which one must find a way.
ex: The tourists got completely lost inside the historic city's maze of narrow winding cobblestone streets.
nat: Navigating the maze of federal tax regulations requires consulting an experienced certified public accountant.

mis.bad: We entered into a hedge maze.
mis.good: We entered a hedge maze.
mis.why: "Enter" takes a direct object without "into": "entered a hedge maze".

def: The intervening time; the period between two events.
ex: The staging build will take twenty minutes; in the meantime, let's grab a quick coffee.
nat: The contractor promised to fix the leak tomorrow, but offered a bucket for the meantime.

mis.bad: On the meantime, we can review the slides.
mis.good: In the meantime, we can review the slides.
mis.why: Always use "in the meantime", never "on the meantime".

def: At the same time; in the intervening period.
ex: Engineers worked frantically to patch the server; meanwhile, customer support agents reassured anxious enterprise clients.
nat: The pasta sauce was simmering on the stove; meanwhile, Carlos chopped fresh salad vegetables.

mis.bad: While that, he finished the presentation.
mis.good: Meanwhile, he finished the presentation / In the meantime, he finished.
mis.why: Do not translate "enquanto isso" as "while that"; use "meanwhile" or "in the meantime".

def: A person who repairs and maintains machinery, especially motor vehicles.
ex: Take your car to a certified mechanic as soon as the check-engine light turns on.
nat: The experienced aircraft mechanic performed a thorough pre-flight safety inspection of the jet turbine.

mis.bad: He works as mechanical in the garage.
mis.good: He works as a mechanic in the garage.
mis.why: The person is a "mechanic"; "mechanical" is an adjective.

def: Operated by a machine or mechanism; relating to machines.
ex: The vintage watch uses an intricate mechanical spring movement rather than modern quartz electronic batteries.
nat: A sudden mechanical failure forced the cargo airplane to make an emergency landing yesterday.

mis.bad: He works in the mechanic engineering department.
mis.good: He works in the mechanical engineering department.
mis.why: Use the adjective "mechanical" before "engineering", not the noun "mechanic".

def: A system of parts working together in a machine; a piece of machinery or natural process.
ex: The locking mechanism inside the hotel safe jammed, requiring a maintenance technician to open it.
nat: Scientists discovered the exact biological mechanism by which cancer cells resist standard chemotherapy drugs.

mis.bad: He uses humor as a mechanism of defense.
mis.good: He uses humor as a defense mechanism.
mis.why: Use the compound noun "defense mechanism", not "mechanism of defense".

def: A metal disc awarded as a distinction for actions or victory in sports competitions.
ex: The Brazilian gymnast wept tears of joy after winning the Olympic gold medal in Paris.
nat: Veterans proudly wore their service medals on their lapels during the memorial day parade.

mis.bad: He won a gold meddle in the tournament.
mis.good: He won a gold medal in the tournament.
mis.why: Do not confuse "medal" (award) with "meddle" (interfere) or "metal" (material).

def: The main means of mass communication regarded collectively.
ex: Social media platforms have transformed how modern consumers discover new products and connect online.
nat: The controversial courtroom trial received intense coverage across national media outlets throughout the week.

mis.bad: The medias are reporting the story.
mis.good: The media is / media are reporting the story.
mis.why: "Media" is plural in form (from medium) and functions collectively; do not say "the medias".

def: A substance used for medical treatment, especially a medicine or drug.
ex: Always take your prescription blood pressure medication with a glass of water every morning.
nat: The patient experienced mild drowsiness as a side effect of the newly prescribed medication.

mis.bad: I took many medications for my headache.
mis.good: I took medication for my headache / took some medication.
mis.why: "Medication" is often treated as uncountable; say "took some medication" or "took painkillers".

def: The science or practice of diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of disease, or a therapeutic substance.
ex: She decided to study medicine at university because of her strong desire to heal people.
nat: Store liquid cough medicine in a cool, dry place out of reach of children.

mis.bad: He gave me a good remedy for my flu.
mis.good: He gave me good medicine for my flu / recommended a good medicine.
mis.why: In Portuguese "remédio" usually translates to "medicine" or "medication", while English "remedy" often implies a home or natural solution.

def: Relating to the Middle Ages, or antiquated and old-fashioned.
ex: Tourists walked along the towering stone walls of the preserved medieval castle in southern France.
nat: The computer system at the municipal licensing office felt completely medieval compared to modern apps.

mis.bad: The village has a medieval style of architecture.
mis.good: The village has medieval architecture.
mis.why: Use "medieval" directly as an adjective modifying "architecture".

def: To focus one's mind for a period of time, in silence or with chanting, for relaxation.
ex: She likes to meditate for fifteen quiet minutes every morning before opening her work emails.
nat: Philosophers often meditate on deep ethical questions regarding technological advances and human nature.

mis.bad: He meditated about the problem all night.
mis.good: He meditated on the problem all night / contemplated the problem.
mis.why: The preposition used with "meditate" is "on", not "about".

def: The practice of meditating, or a continuous and profound contemplation on a subject.
ex: Daily mindfulness meditation has been shown to reduce chronic psychological stress and lower blood pressure.
nat: She attended a weekend silent meditation retreat in the mountains to recharge her mental energy.

mis.bad: She made a meditation this morning.
mis.good: She practiced meditation this morning / she meditated this morning.
mis.why: Use "practice meditation" or the verb "meditate", never "make a meditation".

def: About halfway between two extremes of size or degree; average.
ex: He ordered a grilled burger cooked to medium doneness with seasoned french fries on the side.
nat: Small and medium enterprises form the economic backbone of employment across Latin American economies.

mis.bad: I wear a size middle in shirts.
mis.good: I wear a size medium in shirts.
mis.why: For clothing sizes, always use "medium", never "middle".

def: Quiet, gentle, and easily imposed on; submissive.
ex: The meek customer service representative rarely pushed back when clients made unreasonable and loud demands.
nat: Do not mistake her quiet and meek demeanor for a lack of fierce internal determination.

mis.bad: He was very meek to speak.
mis.good: He was too meek to speak up.
mis.why: Say "too meek to speak up" for someone afraid to assert themselves.

def: A feeling of pensive sadness, typically with no obvious cause; or causing sadness.
ex: The cellist played a melancholy melody that brought tears to the eyes of the audience.
nat: Walking through the rain-soaked empty autumn park filled him with a quiet, pensive melancholy.

mis.bad: He was in a melancholic state of mind.
mis.good: He was in a melancholy mood / felt melancholy.
mis.why: In modern English, "melancholy" is preferred as both adjective and noun.

def: Pleasantly smooth or soft in sound, taste, or character; relaxed.
ex: The acoustic coffee shop played mellow jazz music that created an ideal remote working atmosphere.
nat: As the red wine ages in oak barrels, it develops a delightfully rich, mellow flavor.

mis.bad: The sound of his voice is very melow.
mis.good: The sound of his voice is very mellow.
mis.why: Watch the spelling: "mellow" has double "l".

def: A sequence of single notes that is musically satisfying; a tune.
ex: The catchy piano melody stayed stuck in my head for the rest of the day.
nat: She hummed a sweet folk melody while watering the blossoming geranium plants on her balcony.

mis.bad: He whistled the music of the film.
mis.good: He whistled the melody of the film / whistled the theme tune.
mis.why: Use "melody" or "tune" for the specific sequence of notes whistled or hummed.

def: To make or become liquefied by heat.
ex: Rising global temperatures cause polar ice sheets to melt at an unprecedented and alarming rate.
nat: Gently melt two tablespoons of unsalted butter in a hot skillet before adding the eggs.

mis.bad: The ice melted into water by the sun.
mis.good: The ice melted in the sun.
mis.why: Say "melted in the sun", not "by the sun".

def: The state of being a member of a group or organization.
ex: You must renew your annual gym membership before the end of this month to avoid penalties.
nat: The museum offers discounted family membership packages with free entry to special temporary cultural exhibitions.

mis.bad: I canceled my association in the gym.
mis.good: I canceled my gym membership.
mis.why: Do not translate "associação à academia" as "association"; use "gym membership".

def: A written message in business or diplomacy.
ex: The CEO sent an urgent internal memo clarifying the updated hybrid remote working policy yesterday.
nat: Please read the security memo before connecting personal mobile devices to the corporate private network.

mis.bad: The boss sent a memorand to all.
mis.good: The boss sent a memo to all staff.
mis.why: The natural common word in business English is "memo", not "memorand".

def: Easily remembered, especially because of being special or unusual.
ex: Our road trip through the national parks of Utah was an extraordinarily memorable family adventure.
nat: The keynote speaker closed her inspiring presentation with a memorable quote about lifelong continuous learning.

mis.bad: It was an unforgettable and memorable time.
mis.good: It was a memorable time / truly memorable experience.
mis.why: Avoid piling up identical adjectives like "unforgettable and memorable".

def: A statue or other structure established to remind people of a person or event.
ex: Citizens gathered at the national marble memorial to honor veterans who died during the war.
nat: The city council decided to erect a memorial plaque in tribute to the civic hero.

mis.bad: They attended to the memorial service.
mis.good: They attended the memorial service.
mis.why: "Attend" takes a direct object without "to": "attended the memorial service".

def: A person or thing that is likely to cause harm; a threat or danger.
ex: Reckless drivers speeding through quiet school zones are a constant menace to pedestrian child safety.
nat: Untreated industrial waste dumping poses an acute ecological menace to local freshwater river basins.

mis.bad: He was a menace for the neighborhood.
mis.good: He was a menace to the neighborhood.
mis.why: Use "a menace to [someone/something]", not "for".

def: To repair something that is broken or damaged, or improve a strained relationship.
ex: She used a needle and strong matching thread to mend the torn jacket pocket seam.
nat: The two rival co-founders scheduled a dinner to try and mend their damaged professional relationship.

mis.bad: The patient is in the mend.
mis.good: The patient is on the mend.
mis.why: The correct idiom for recovering health is "on the mend", not "in the mend".

def: Relating to the mind, or relating to the disorders of the mind.
ex: Prioritizing sleep and regular breaks is vital for maintaining good mental health during intense projects.
nat: Solving complex algorithmic puzzles requires tremendous mental stamina and sharp analytical thinking from engineers.

mis.bad: He had a mental problem of stress.
mis.good: He had mental stress / struggled with his mental health.
mis.why: Avoid stigmatizing phrasing like "a mental problem of stress"; use "struggled with mental health".

def: The guidance provided by a mentor, especially an experienced person in a company.
ex: Joining the corporate engineering mentorship program helped new hires integrate into teams much faster.
nat: She expressed deep gratitude for her director's generous career mentorship over the past five years.

mis.bad: I received a good mentoring of him.
mis.good: I received good mentorship from him.
mis.why: Use "mentorship from [someone]", not "mentoring of him".

def: A professional soldier hired to serve in a foreign army, or an opportunistic person.
ex: The authoritarian regime hired foreign mercenaries to protect valuable diamond mines against rebel militia forces.
nat: He was criticized as a corporate mercenary who moved from startup to startup solely for bonuses.

mis.bad: He is very mercenary about his friends.
mis.good: He has a mercenary attitude toward friendship.
mis.why: Collocate naturally with "mercenary attitude toward".

def: Showing no mercy; cruel and without pity.
ex: The desert sun was merciless, beating down on the stranded hikers with blistering midday heat.
nat: The sports media was merciless in criticizing the national soccer coach following the embarrassing defeat.

mis.bad: The critic was merciless with the novel.
mis.good: The critic was merciless in his criticism of the novel.
mis.why: Say "merciless in [action]" rather than "merciless with".

def: To combine or cause to combine to form a single entity, or join traffic.
ex: Drivers must yield carefully before attempting to merge onto the crowded morning commuter expressway lanes.
nat: The lead engineer approved the pull request and merged the code into the main branch.

mis.bad: The road merged with into the highway.
mis.good: The road merged into the highway.
mis.why: Use "merge into" or "merge with", never combine them as "with into".

def: The quality of being particularly good or worthy, especially so as to deserve praise.
ex: Promotions at the engineering company are awarded strictly on technical merit rather than office politics.
nat: Each startup funding proposal will be evaluated thoroughly on its own individual economic merits.

mis.bad: He got promoted by his merits.
mis.good: He was promoted on merit.
mis.why: The standard idiom is "promoted on merit", not "by his merits".

def: Cheerful and lively; festive.
ex: Carolers sang merry holiday songs outside the town hall while snowflakes fell on the square.
nat: The festive pub was filled with merry laughter and the clinking of cold beer mugs.

mis.bad: We wished everyone a happy and merry.
mis.good: We wished everyone a Merry Christmas / happy holiday.
mis.why: "Merry" is predominantly used in the formula "Merry Christmas" or before nouns like "merry mood".

def: To entangle or fit together, or work harmoniously together.
ex: Her practical managerial experience meshed perfectly with his creative engineering vision for the product.
nat: Make sure the metal gear teeth mesh cleanly without grinding before tightening the motor bolts.

mis.bad: Their ideas meshed to each other.
mis.good: Their ideas meshed with each other.
mis.why: Use "mesh with [something]", not "mesh to".

def: A dirty or untidy state of things or of a place, or a difficult predicament.
ex: Clean up the mess in your bedroom before our dinner guests arrive this evening.
nat: The canceled merger left the bank's corporate balance sheet in a complete financial mess.

mis.bad: He made a big bagunça in the kitchen.
mis.good: He made a big mess in the kitchen.
mis.why: Translate Portuguese "bagunça" as "mess" in English.

def: Untidy or dirty, or generating confusion and unpleasant complications.
ex: Working at a messy desk cluttered with old coffee mugs hurts your daily creative focus.
nat: The legal divorce proceedings became extraordinarily messy as both parties fought over intellectual property.

mis.bad: His room is very mess.
mis.good: His room is very messy.
mis.why: Use the adjective "messy" after "is", not the noun "mess".

def: A figure of speech in which a word or phrase is applied to an object or action.
ex: The speaker used an extended nautical navigation metaphor to explain company organizational restructuring decisions.
nat: Calling life a journey across stormy seas is an ancient and universally recognized literary metaphor.

mis.bad: It was a metaphoric phrase.
mis.good: It was a metaphorical phrase / a metaphor.
mis.why: The standard adjective is "metaphorical", not "metaphoric".

def: A small body of matter from outer space that enters the earth's atmosphere.
ex: Campers were thrilled to see a brilliant green meteor streak across the clear midnight sky.
nat: The annual Perseid meteor shower produces dozens of visible shooting trails every August night.

mis.bad: We saw a falling meteorite in the sky.
mis.good: We saw a meteor streak across the sky.
mis.why: A "meteor" is the streak of light in the sky; a "meteorite" is the rock that hits the ground.

def: Done according to a systematic or established form of procedure.
ex: Finding obscure multithreaded software bugs requires a calm, disciplined, and methodical debugging approach.
nat: The detective conducted a methodical search of the crime scene, collecting microscopic forensic evidence.

mis.bad: He works in a methodic way.
mis.good: He works in a methodical way / is very methodical.
mis.why: Use "methodical", not "methodic".

def: The capital or chief city of a country or region; a very large city.
ex: São Paulo is a sprawling metropolis of over twenty million people with vibrant cultural diversity.
nat: High-speed rail links connecting the booming regional metropolis to coastal ports boosted foreign trade.

mis.bad: He moved to the big metropole.
mis.good: He moved to the big metropolis.
mis.why: In English, spell and say "metropolis", not "metropole".

def: The middle of the day; noon.
ex: Tourists in Mediterranean coastal towns usually take a quiet indoor rest during the hot midday heat.
nat: The construction crew took their lunch break at midday under the shade of olive trees.

mis.bad: We had lunch in the midday.
mis.good: We had lunch at midday / at noon.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "at": "at midday", not "in the midday".

def: At an equal distance from the extremes or outer limits; central.
ex: Sitting in the middle seat on a twelve-hour international flight is notoriously uncomfortable for travelers.
nat: The documentary explores the economic struggles of middle class families in changing post-industrial cities.

mis.bad: He sat in the center seat of the plane.
mis.good: He sat in the middle seat on the plane.
mis.why: Use "middle seat" on planes or trains, not "center seat".

def: Twelve o'clock at night.
ex: Engineers deployed the crucial database software migration patch at midnight when network traffic was lowest.
nat: The new fantasy novel went on sale at midnight to hundreds of eager waiting fans.

mis.bad: The party ended in the midnight.
mis.good: The party ended at midnight.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "at": "at midnight", never "in the midnight".

def: The middle point or part; or used in prepositional phrases meaning surrounded by.
ex: We found ourselves in the midst of a massive thunderstorm without any waterproof umbrellas.
nat: She remained remarkably calm even in the midst of intense corporate crisis management meetings.

mis.bad: He arrived in the middle of our midst.
mis.good: He arrived in our midst / in the midst of the crisis.
mis.why: Say "in our midst" or "in the midst of [a situation]".

def: Possessing great and impressive power or strength, especially on account of size.
ex: The mighty Amazon River flows thousands of miles through dense tropical rainforests into the Atlantic.
nat: With one mighty swing of the bat, the baseball player sent the ball into the stands.

mis.bad: The river has a mighty flow of water.
mis.good: The mighty river flows toward the ocean.
mis.why: Use "mighty" naturally as an attributive adjective before the noun.

def: A person who moves from one place to another, especially in order to find work.
ex: Thousands of seasonal migrant workers arrive in California each spring to harvest fruit crops.
nat: The humanitarian charity distributed food, blankets, and clean drinking water to arriving migrant families.

mis.bad: The migrant arrived in the country yesterday.
mis.good: The migrant arrived in the country yesterday / many migrant workers arrived.
mis.why: Note: "migrant" can be seasonal or temporary, whereas "immigrant" usually implies settling permanently.

def: Movement from one part of something to another, or movement of animals or software data.
ex: The scheduled cloud database migration went smoothly with less than five minutes of total downtime.
nat: The seasonal migration of millions of monarch butterflies across North America is an extraordinary spectacle.

mis.bad: We executed the migration of database.
mis.good: We executed the database migration.
mis.why: Use the compound noun "database migration" in technical contexts.

def: Not severe, serious, or harsh; gentle and not sharp.
ex: San Diego is famous for its mild winter temperatures and abundant coastal sunny days.
nat: The doctor confirmed that the patient was experiencing only mild seasonal allergy symptoms.

mis.bad: The climate here is very suave.
mis.good: The climate here is very mild.
mis.why: Do not translate Portuguese "suave" as "suave" for weather; use "mild".

def: Combative and aggressive in support of a political or social cause.
ex: The labor union took a militant stance during wage negotiations, threatening an immediate nationwide strike.
nat: Security agencies monitored militant extremist groups attempting to recruit vulnerable youths online.

mis.bad: He is a political militant of the party.
mis.good: He is a political activist / militant party member.
mis.why: In English, "militant" often carries aggressive or extremist connotations; for peaceful activism use "activist".

def: Relating to or characteristic of soldiers or armed forces.
ex: Modern military aircraft utilize advanced radar-absorbent materials to avoid detection by hostile defense systems.
nat: She completed four years of honorable military service before enrolling in university software engineering.

mis.bad: He served in the army military.
mis.good: He served in the military / in the army.
mis.why: Say "in the military" or "in the army", not "army military".

def: To imitate someone or their actions or words, especially in order to entertain or ridicule.
ex: Large neural language models can mimic human conversational styles with surprising and nuanced accuracy.
nat: Chameleons alter their skin pigmentation to mimic the surrounding tree leaves and branches.

mis.bad: He mimicked to his teacher.
mis.good: He mimicked his teacher.
mis.why: "Mimic" is a transitive verb; do not use the preposition "to".

def: To reduce something to the smallest possible amount or degree.
ex: Wearing seatbelts and following the speed limit helps minimize the risk of serious injury.
nat: The product team decided to minimize latency by deploying edge servers across South America.

mis.bad: We need to minimize down the costs.
mis.good: We need to minimize costs.
mis.why: Do not add "down" after "minimize".

def: The lowest or smallest quantity, amount, or degree attainable.
ex: Employees working in the state must receive at least the legal minimum hourly wage.
nat: The airline requires a minimum connection time of ninety minutes for international passenger transfers.

mis.bad: The minimal wage was increased this month.
mis.good: The minimum wage was increased this month.
mis.why: In English, use "minimum wage", not "minimal wage".

def: A government department headed by a minister of state.
ex: The Ministry of Education announced new public funding for computer programming classes in schools.
nat: Representatives from the finance ministry met with regional bankers to discuss inflation management strategies.

mis.bad: He works in the minister of health.
mis.good: He works in the Ministry of Health.
mis.why: The government department is the "Ministry"; the person heading it is the "Minister".

def: A surprising and welcome event that is not explicable by natural or scientific laws.
ex: It was an absolute miracle that all passengers walked away unharmed from the crash.
nat: Modern medical advancements like vaccines are often described as scientific miracles for public health.

mis.bad: It happened by miracle.
mis.good: It was a miracle / It happened miraculously.
mis.why: Use "it was a miracle" or the adverb "miraculously", not "by miracle".

def: Of the nature of a miracle; bringing about a very welcome or improbable result.
ex: The injured athlete made a truly miraculous recovery and competed in the finals yesterday.
nat: Rescue crews described finding the stranded puppy alive after two weeks as completely miraculous.

mis.bad: He had a miraculous in his recovery.
mis.good: His recovery was miraculous / He made a miraculous recovery.
mis.why: Use "miraculous" as an adjective, not a standalone noun.

def: An optical illusion caused by atmospheric conditions, or an unrealistic hope.
ex: Thirsty travelers in the desert were deceived by a shimmering mirage of cool water.
nat: The promise of overnight wealth from speculative trading turned out to be pure mirage.

mis.bad: The lake was just an optical mirage.
mis.good: The lake was just a mirage.
mis.why: Say "a mirage" directly without repeating "optical" unnecessarily.

def: A reflective surface that bounces light to form an image of an object.
ex: Always adjust your rearview mirror and side mirrors before driving out onto public roads.
nat: Literature and cinema often function as a cultural mirror reflecting the anxieties of society.

mis.bad: Look at the mirror.
mis.good: Look in the mirror.
mis.why: When looking at your own reflection, say "look in the mirror".

def: To behave badly or in an improper manner.
ex: Parents were warned that children who misbehave during the museum tour would be escorted out.
nat: The puppy tends to misbehave and chew up slippers whenever left home alone for hours.

mis.bad: He behaved bad at school today.
mis.good: He misbehaved at school today / behaved badly.
mis.why: Use "misbehaved" or "behaved badly", never "behaved bad".

def: Causing or showing a fondness for causing trouble in a playful way.
ex: The mischievous toddler hid his father's car keys inside a flower pot on the terrace.
nat: She gave me a mischievous smile right before revealing the surprise birthday celebration plans.

mis.bad: He is very mischevious.
mis.good: He is very mischievous.
mis.why: Watch both the spelling and pronunciation: "mischievous" has three syllables, not four.

def: A view or opinion that is incorrect because based on faulty thinking or understanding.
ex: It is a widespread misconception that speaking English fluently requires completely eliminating your foreign accent.
nat: The science documentary corrected common misconceptions regarding how black holes behave in deep space.

mis.bad: He has a misconception on that.
mis.good: He has a misconception about that.
mis.why: Use "misconception about [a topic]", not "on".

def: Unacceptable or improper behavior, especially by an employee or professional person.
ex: The senior executive was immediately fired following an independent internal investigation into corporate financial misconduct.
nat: The physician was sued for professional medical misconduct after prescribing unauthorized experimental drugs.

mis.bad: He committed a serious misconduct.
mis.good: He committed serious misconduct / an act of serious misconduct.
mis.why: "Misconduct" is uncountable; avoid saying "a misconduct".

def: To fail to discharge or fire properly, or fail to produce the intended result.
ex: The marketing campaign misfired badly when consumers criticized the tone-deaf and insensitive advertisements.
nat: If the car engine begins to misfire on acceleration, check the spark plugs immediately.

mis.bad: His plan misfired of success.
mis.good: His plan misfired / backfired.
mis.why: "Misfire" is intransitive; do not add "of success".

def: Bad luck; an unfortunate condition or event.
ex: He had the terrible misfortune of losing his passport the evening before flying abroad.
nat: A series of unexpected financial misfortunes forced the family restaurant to close down permanently.

mis.bad: He had bad misfortune with his job.
mis.good: He had the misfortune to lose his job / suffered misfortune.
mis.why: Avoid saying "bad misfortune", as "misfortune" already implies bad fortune.

def: To interpret something wrongly or incorrectly.
ex: Text messages without emojis can easily cause readers to misinterpret the sender's genuine emotional tone.
nat: The junior analyst misinterpreted the quarterly earnings chart, leading to erroneous financial forecasts.

mis.bad: She misinterpreted about my words.
mis.good: She misinterpreted my words.
mis.why: "Misinterpret" takes a direct object without "about".

def: To form a wrong opinion or conclusion about someone or something.
ex: The driver misjudged the distance between the two vehicles and scraped the passenger door.
nat: Do not misjudge her quiet and thoughtful demeanor as a sign of intellectual weakness.

mis.bad: He misjudged about his competitor.
mis.good: He misjudged his competitor.
mis.why: "Misjudge" is transitive; do not use the preposition "about".

def: To cause someone to have a wrong idea or impression about someone or something.
ex: Advertisers must never mislead consumers with fabricated claims about dietary supplement health benefits.
nat: The ambiguous wording in the software contract was deliberately designed to mislead potential buyers.

mis.bad: The advertisement misled to consumers.
mis.good: The advertisement misled consumers.
mis.why: "Mislead" takes a direct object without "to".

def: A failure to correspond or match; a discrepancy.
ex: There is a serious mismatch between developer skill sets and current employer artificial intelligence demands.
nat: The tennis final proved to be a total mismatch between the champion and the novice.

mis.bad: There is a mismatch of skills with the job.
mis.good: There is a skills mismatch for the job / mismatch between skills and job requirements.
mis.why: Use "mismatch between A and B", not "mismatch of A with B".

def: A cloud of tiny water droplets suspended in the atmosphere at or near the earth's surface.
ex: A thick morning mist hung over the calm lake until the warm sunshine dispersed it.
nat: Waterfalls create a refreshing fine mist that cools hikers standing along the scenic canyon trails.

mis.bad: The mountain was covered by a fog mist.
mis.good: The mountain was shrouded in mist.
mis.why: Do not combine "fog mist"; use either "mist" (lighter) or "fog" (denser).

def: An action or judgment that is misguided or wrong.
ex: Making a grammatical mistake while practicing speaking English is completely normal and helps you learn.
nat: The bank apologized for the billing mistake and credited the fifty-dollar fee back immediately.

mis.bad: I did a mistake in the test.
mis.good: I made a mistake on the test.
mis.why: Always use the collocation "make a mistake", never "do a mistake".

def: To be suspicious of; have no confidence in.
ex: Citizens began to mistrust official statements after conflicting reports emerged from independent journalistic investigators.
nat: Consumers often mistrust unfamiliar shopping websites that lack verifiable customer reviews and secure payment options.

mis.bad: I mistrust from that online store.
mis.good: I mistrust that online store.
mis.why: "Mistrust" is a transitive verb; omit the preposition "from".

def: To make a long, low sound expressing physical or mental suffering, or complain.
ex: Coworkers who constantly moan about office trivialities create a toxic and demotivating team environment.
nat: The injured soccer player moaned in pain while holding his twisted right knee tightly.

mis.bad: He moaned of the heavy workload.
mis.good: He moaned about the heavy workload.
mis.why: Use "moan about [something]", not "moan of".

def: A large crowd of people, especially one that is disorderly and intent on causing trouble.
ex: An angry mob of protesters gathered outside the embassy gates demanding an immediate formal response.
nat: Security officers escorted the famous movie star safely away from the mob of eager photographers.

mis.bad: A big mob of people entered.
mis.good: An angry mob gathered outside.
mis.why: "Mob" usually implies disorder or aggression; for a neutral large gathering use "crowd".

def: Able to move or be moved freely or easily.
ex: Most online banking users prefer managing their checking and savings accounts through native mobile apps.
nat: The emergency dental clinic operates a mobile medical van to treat patients in remote villages.

mis.bad: I answered from my mobile phone device.
mis.good: I answered from my mobile phone / mobile device.
mis.why: Say "mobile phone" or "mobile device", not "mobile phone device".

def: The ability to move or be moved freely and easily.
ex: Performing regular hip mobility exercises helps office workers prevent chronic lower back stiffness and pain.
nat: Investing in public subway infrastructure improves social mobility and economic opportunity for suburban residents.

mis.bad: He has a good mobility of legs.
mis.good: He has good leg mobility / good joint mobility.
mis.why: Say "good joint mobility" or "leg mobility" rather than "mobility of legs".

def: To prepare and organize troops or resources for active service or a campaign.
ex: The international community acted swiftly to mobilize humanitarian emergency aid for the earthquake victims.
nat: Environmental activists managed to mobilize thousands of college students for the worldwide climate strike.

mis.bad: The city mobilized to support for the victims.
mis.good: The city mobilized support for the victims.
mis.why: "Mobilize" takes a direct object: "mobilized support for the victims".

def: To tease or laugh at in a scornful or contemptuous manner.
ex: It is cruel and unprofessional to mock colleagues when they make honest language errors.
nat: Comedians frequently mock political figures and absurd cultural trends during their weekly satirical monologues.

mis.bad: He mocked of his brother's haircut.
mis.good: He mocked his brother's haircut.
mis.why: "Mock" is a transitive verb; omit the preposition "of".

def: A model or replica of a machine or structure, used for instructional or design purposes.
ex: The UX designer presented a clickable interactive mock-up of the mobile checkout flow yesterday.
nat: Before manufacturing the hardware casing, engineers built a physical wooden mock-up for testing.

mis.bad: The designer made a mock up of the screen.
mis.good: The designer made a mock-up of the screen.
mis.why: As a noun, hyphenate as "mock-up" (or write "mockup").

def: A way or manner in which something occurs or is experienced; a state of operation.
ex: Switching your smartphone to airplane mode before takeoff saves valuable battery life during flights.
nat: Rail transport remains the most environmentally sustainable mode of intercity passenger and freight travel.

mis.bad: Turn the phone in dark mode.
mis.good: Turn the phone to dark mode / switch to dark mode.
mis.why: Use "switch to [mode]" or "in [mode]": "switch to dark mode".

def: Average in amount, intensity, quality, or degree; neither small nor large.
ex: Doctors recommend at least one hundred fifty minutes of moderate cardiovascular aerobic exercise weekly.
nat: The hotel offers clean, comfortable rooms and high-speed Wi-Fi at a very moderate price.

mis.bad: He exercises with a moderate intensely.
mis.good: He exercises at a moderate intensity.
mis.why: Say "at a moderate intensity / pace".

def: The process of adapting something to modern needs or habits.
ex: The comprehensive modernization of the public subway network significantly reduced daily commuter delay times.
nat: Banks are spending billions on infrastructure modernization to replace legacy mainframe software with cloud systems.

mis.bad: The modernization of the system was fastly done.
mis.good: The modernization of the system was quickly completed.
mis.why: Use "quickly completed", not "fastly done" ("fastly" does not exist).

def: To adapt something to modern needs or habits, typically by installing modern technology.
ex: The regional manufacturing plant decided to modernize its assembly line with automated robotic machinery.
nat: Small business owners must modernize their payment systems to accept contactless credit cards easily.

mis.bad: We need to modernizate our tools.
mis.good: We need to modernize our tools.
mis.why: The correct English verb is "modernize", not "modernizate".

def: To make partial or minor changes to something, typically so as to improve it.
ex: You should modify the default database password immediately after installing the software on servers.
nat: The architect had to modify the original blueprints to comply with local earthquake building codes.

mis.bad: We modified about the contract clauses.
mis.good: We modified the contract clauses.
mis.why: "Modify" is a transitive verb; omit the preposition "about".

def: Employing or involving a module or modules as the basis of design or construction.
ex: Writing clean, modular code allows software engineering teams to deploy independent features without system disruptions.
nat: The apartment building was constructed rapidly using prefabricated modular steel and concrete units.

mis.bad: The program has a very module structure.
mis.good: The program has a very modular structure.
mis.why: Use the adjective "modular", not the noun "module", before "structure".

def: Water or other liquid diffused in a small quantity as vapor, within a solid, or on a surface.
ex: Excess moisture inside closed basement rooms can encourage dangerous black mold to grow rapidly.
nat: Using a gentle hydrating face cream locks in essential moisture during dry winter weather.

mis.bad: There was too much humidity moisture on the walls.
mis.good: There was too much moisture on the walls.
mis.why: Do not combine "humidity moisture"; use "moisture" for physical wetness on surfaces.

def: Relating to money or to the mechanisms by which money is supplied and circulated.
ex: The central bank adjusted its monetary policy by raising benchmark interest rates to combat inflation.
nat: The antique family violin had little monetary value but carried immense irreplaceable emotional worth.

mis.bad: The prize had an enormous monetary worth value.
mis.good: The prize had enormous monetary value.
mis.why: Say "monetary value", not "monetary worth value".

def: The exclusive possession or control of the supply of or trade in a commodity or service.
ex: Antitrust regulators sued the multinational tech company to prevent it from maintaining an illegal monopoly.
nat: The state maintained a strict monopoly on postal mail delivery services for over a century.

mis.bad: The firm has a monopoly on the market.
mis.good: The firm has a monopoly in / over the market.
mis.why: Collocate with "monopoly over" or "monopoly in the market", or "monopoly on supply".

def: Dull, tedious, and repetitious; lacking in variety and interest.
ex: Listening to a speaker with a monotonous voice for two hours makes staying awake challenging.
nat: Data entry can feel painfully monotonous when you are typing identical numbers into spreadsheets daily.

mis.bad: The work was very monotonously.
mis.good: The work was very monotonous.
mis.why: Use the adjective "monotonous" after "was", not the adverb form.

def: Having the ugly or frightening appearance of a monster; or shockingly hideous or wrong.
ex: Dumping toxic untreated chemical waste into pristine drinking reservoirs is a monstrous crime against humanity.
nat: The hurricane generated monstrous twenty-foot ocean waves that battered the coastal sea wall all night.

mis.bad: It was a monstrous of an error.
mis.good: It was a monstrous error.
mis.why: Use "monstrous" directly as an adjective before the noun.

def: Done, produced, or occurring once every month.
ex: Our company holds a monthly all-hands meeting to review product milestones and celebrate achievements.
nat: Paying your full monthly credit card balance on time prevents costly accumulated interest charges.

mis.bad: I pay a fee monthly of fifty dollars.
mis.good: I pay a monthly fee of fifty dollars.
mis.why: Place the adjective "monthly" before the noun: "monthly fee".

def: Great in importance, extent, or size; or serving as a monument.
ex: Mapping the complete human genome was a monumental scientific achievement that revolutionized personalized medical treatments.
nat: The architecture firm designed a monumental glass tower that transformed the capital's skyline forever.

mis.bad: It was a monumental of a project.
mis.good: It was a monumental project / monumental achievement.
mis.why: Use "monumental" directly as an adjective: "a monumental task".

def: A temporary state of mind or feeling.
ex: A brisk twenty-minute walk in natural morning sunlight can noticeably lift your overall mood.
nat: I am not in the mood to attend another loud networking party this evening.

mis.bad: I am not on the mood to go out.
mis.good: I am not in the mood to go out.
mis.why: Always say "in the mood", never "on the mood".

def: Concerned with the principles of right and wrong behavior and the goodness or badness.
ex: Scientists have a clear moral responsibility to consider the ethical consequences of their technical innovations.
nat: The fable of the tortoise and the hare teaches a timeless moral lesson about perseverance.

mis.bad: He gave me morale support during the exam.
mis.good: He gave me moral support during the exam.
mis.why: Do not confuse "moral" (ethical) with "morale" (confidence/spirit).

def: As a further matter; besides; in addition.
ex: The proposed software solution is expensive; moreover, it fails to solve our core scalability problems.
nat: Cycling to work saves daily commuting money; moreover, it provides excellent regular cardiovascular exercise.

mis.bad: The project was delayed, more over, it was over budget.
mis.good: The project was delayed; moreover, it was over budget.
mis.why: Write "moreover" as one single word, not two separate words.

def: Living human beings subject to death; causing death; fatal.
ex: Every human being on this earth is mortal, which makes our limited time deeply precious.
nat: The brave medieval knight sustained a mortal wound during the fierce castle battle yesterday.

mis.bad: He escaped from a mortally danger.
mis.good: He escaped from mortal danger.
mis.why: Use the adjective "mortal" before the noun "danger", not the adverb.
